content:
Lists of "priests who became Muslim" pass from website to website, and Christian critics answer them with a fair charge: the titles grow with each retelling. A church volunteer becomes a pastor, a pastor becomes a bishop, and a quotation appears that no one can trace.

The charge is right about the lists and wrong about the people behind the best of them. Some Christian ministers and priests did embrace Islam, and their former office is on record in their own words, in obituaries and in scholarly reference works.

This article aims to provide context to those stories, insha'Allah, in five cases where the former Christian role can be documented, each given at the strength its sources allow. The Quran sets the terms for every such choice: "Let there be no compulsion in religion: Truth stands out clear from Error" (2:256).[1]

The best documented case is also the oldest. Christian-Muslim Relations: A Bibliographical History, the reference work edited by David Thomas and John Chesworth, describes him as "a former Roman Catholic priest of the Uniate-Chaldean Church" who took the name ʿAbd al-Aḥad, "Servant of the One", when he became Muslim.[2]

He was born in Urmia, in Iran, in 1867. He studied in Rome at the Pontificio Collegio Urbano and was ordained priest in 1895. A letter of 14 February 1900, printed in The Tablet, is signed "David Benjamin, Archpriest of Urmia".[2]

The entry also gives what the popular lists leave out. He left the priesthood in 1900, joined the Unitarians in England in 1903, and embraced Islam in Istanbul in 1904, after meeting the Shaykh al-Islam, Mehmed Cemaleddin Efendi.[2] He later wrote Muhammad in the Bible. Some websites call him a bishop; the record gives priest and archpriest, and that is enough.

Yusuf Estes was born in Texas in 1944. His foundation describes "three decades preaching, teaching music ministry, and building businesses across Texas, Oklahoma and Florida", and states: "An American minister spent thirty years preaching Christianity. In 1991 he entered Islam."[3]

His own account begins early in 1991, when his father's business brought him a man from Egypt whom he hoped to convert. The conversations ran the other way.[3] He later served as a Muslim chaplain for the United States Bureau of Prisons.[3]

These pages are his foundation's own, and they are the source for his story. We call him what they call him, a minister and preacher, and claim no more.

Jerald Dirks is documented in detail. "In 1969, he obtained his License to Preach from the United Methodist Church, and he was ordained into the Christian ministry (deaconate) by the United Methodist Church in 1972." He took his Master of Divinity at Harvard Divinity School in 1974 and a doctorate in clinical psychology at the University of Denver in 1978.[4]

"He converted to Islam in 1993." He died on 14 January 2019.[4] Between those dates he wrote several books on Islam and Christianity, and his own account describes a long reconsideration that began with questions raised in seminary.

His Harvard degree shows that he knew Christian theology from the inside. His conclusions stand or fall on the arguments in his books, which is where he placed them.

Kenneth Jenkins tells his own story. Arab News introduced it in 2014: "Kenneth L. Jenkins was former minister and elder of church in Indiana, US." In his words: "I acknowledged my call to the ministry at the age of 20."[5]

He moved to Saudi Arabia for work, and writes that he saw "an immediate difference in the lifestyle of the Muslim people." After watching the debate between Ahmed Deedat and Jimmy Swaggart, "I immediately became a Muslim." He then declared his Islam formally at the office of Shaykh Ibn Baz.[6]

The account is autobiography. It is good evidence of what he lived through and what he believed, and we quote it as his.

Idris Tawfiq was a British writer who, in the words of his publisher, "for many years, was head of religious education in different schools in the United Kingdom. Before embracing Islam, he was a Roman Catholic priest." He died in February 2016.[7]

He was careful about the order of events: "In my own case, I left the ministry and I left the Church before embracing Islam."[7] In his own account, "I enjoyed being a priest helping the people for some years. However, deep inside I was not happy and I felt that there was something not right."[8]

A holiday in Egypt drew him to Islam. Back in London, he went to London Central Mosque, where he met Yusuf Islam and recited the declaration of faith after him in Arabic.[8] He left the priesthood first and embraced Islam later, and the record should say so.

The bottom line

A conversion proves that a person found the case for Islam convincing. It proves nothing on its own about the case itself, since people also leave Islam for Christianity. The argument for Islam rests on God, revelation and the prophets, and the Quran puts it there: "Say: 'Produce your proof if ye are truthful'" (2:111).[1]

Scholars of conversion warn against reading one cause into a life. Thomas Sealy's study of British converts examines continuity as well as change in their religious identity, and Karin van Nieuwkerk's study of Dutch converts reads conversion through biography and choice.[9] Iulian Vamanu and Elysia Guzik examine what reading meant in recent conversion narratives in both faiths.[9]

Five people with documented Christian ministries embraced Islam: Keldani, an archpriest of Urmia; Estes, a Texas preacher; Dirks, a United Methodist deacon; Jenkins, a Pentecostal minister and elder; and Tawfiq, a Catholic priest. Each case is told here at the strength of its sources, and none needs the inflated titles of the popular lists.

Their stories show sincere people weighing two faiths and choosing freely. The Quran asks the same of every reader, and leaves the choice where it belongs: "Say, 'The truth is from your Lord': Let him who will believe, and let him who will, reject (it)" (18:29).[1] Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Quran 2:111; 2:256; 18:29, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  2. Betül Avcı, "ʿAbd al-Aḥad Dāwūd", in Christian-Muslim Relations: A Bibliographical History, vol. 18, The Ottoman Empire (1800–1914), ed. David Thomas and John Chesworth (Leiden: Brill, 2021), pp. 223–236.
  3. Yusuf Estes, "From Preacher to Muslim", "About" and "A Man from Egypt", yusufestes.com.
  4. "Missionary-Turned-Muslim Scholar Passes Away", AboutIslam, 15 January 2019.
  5. "My Journey from Darkness to Light", Arab News, 8 August 2014.
  6. Kenneth L. Jenkins, "Kenneth L. Jenkins, Minister and Elder of Pentecostal Church, USA (part 3 of 3)", IslamReligion.com, 16 January 2006.
  7. Idris Tawfiq, "Can a Muslim Be a Priest?", AboutIslam, with the author's note.
  8. Idris Tawfiq, "A Former Priest's Journey to Islam", NewMuslim.net.
  9. Thomas Sealy, "British Converts to Islam: Continuity, Change, and Religiosity in Religious Identity", Journal of Contemporary Religion 36, no. 3 (2021), pp. 421–439; Karin van Nieuwkerk, "Biography and Choice: Female Converts to Islam in the Netherlands", Islam and Christian–Muslim Relations 19, no. 4 (2008), pp. 431–447; Iulian Vamanu and Elysia Guzik, "'Closer to God': Meanings of Reading in Recent Conversion Narratives within Christianity and Islam", Journal of Religious & Theological Information 14, nos. 3–4 (2015), pp. 63–78.
